mapName: A Learnable South & West Europe - Identify Every Country

metas.name: Andorra - Architecture
metas.note:
• Andorra has a lot of these stone buildings.
  • They can be seen almost everywhere in the country.

--- NOTE:

  • These buildings can also be found close to Andorra, in the French and Spanish Pyrenees.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/andorra.

metas.name: Andorra - Gen 3 Autumn
metas.note: • All the Generation 3 coverage was taken in October, meaning that many deciduous trees have autumn colours.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/andorra.

metas.name: Azores - Dry Rock Walls
metas.note:
• Dry rock walls made of volcanic rocks are very common on the Azores.

--- NOTE:

  • Dry rock walls are not common on Madeira, and while they are somewhat common on mainland Portugal, they will not be made of volcanic rocks.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Azores - Hydrangeas
metas.note:
• Hydrangeas can commonly be seen on the Azores.

--- NOTE:

  • They can rarely be found on Madeira.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Azores - Landscape
metas.note:
• Most of the Azores visible on Street View consists of open agricultural fields in a rolling landscape, often with taller round hills in the background.

--- NOTE:

  • Madeira has a very mountainous landscape, and very rarely has open agricultural fields.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Belgium - Additional Blue Signs
metas.note:
• Road signs often have an additional small blue sign.
  • In other European countries, these small signs are usually just white.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - Bollards
metas.note:
• Belgium uses white bollards with a yellow rectangular reflector on the front and white on the back.
  • A second type of bollard is dark brown with two red stripes at the top.

--- NOTE:

  • Denmark uses similar white bollards, but they have a red stripe at the top and the reflector is not rectangular.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - Concrete Roads
metas.note:
• A lot of rural roads in Belgium are made out of concrete slabs, almost like you would see in the Philippines or Thailand.

--- NOTE:

  • The Netherlands almost never uses concrete slabs for roads.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - Double Gutters
metas.note:
• Almost all roads (big or small) in Belgium use gutters on both sides.
  • This is much less common in neighbouring countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - Red License Plates
metas.note:
• Licence plates in Belgium use red text.
  • You can recognise this distinct colour even through the blur.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - Small Priority Signs
metas.note: • Priority signs in Belgium have an orange diamond and are much smaller than in other countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - Square Poles
metas.note:
• Most poles in Belgium are concrete, square shaped, and have tiny holes running up them.
  • They often have small metal wrappings around them.
  • The second most common type of pole has oval-shaped holes.

--- NOTE:

  • The small metal wrappings can be found in France as well.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Belgium - Yellow Reflectors
metas.note:
• Belgium uses A-type guardrails with yellow reflectors.

--- NOTE:

  • In Europe, only Spain, Andorra, and Belgium use these reflectors.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/belgium.

metas.name: Croatia - B-Type Guardrails
metas.note:
• Croatia has square (B-type) guardrails.

--- NOTE:

  • Croatia is one of the few European countries that use B-type guardrails.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/croatia.

metas.name: Croatia - Blue Fire Hydrants
metas.note:
• Croatia features blue fire hydrants with two diagonal protrusions on either side.
  • Newer fire hydrants seen in Generation 4 have a smaller top but are still recognisable due to the blue paint.

--- NOTE:

  • Similar fire hydrants can be found in bordering countries, most commonly in Hungary.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/croatia.

metas.name: Croatia - Bollards
metas.note:
• Croatian bollards are white with a black rectangle and red or white reflector.
  • From the top, it is shaped like a triangle.

--- NOTE:

  • Hungarian and Lithuanian bollards look similar, but have more rounded edges compared to Croatia’s sharper edges.
  • Lithuanian bollards will also have an orange reflector.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/croatia.

metas.name: Croatia - Gen 3 Mirror
metas.note:
• Generation 3 coverage often has a non-standard car blur where the side mirrors of the car are partially visible.
  • This is not unique to Croatia, but by far most common there.

--- NOTE:

  • Sometimes, you can see a small circular yellow sticker on the car mirror.
  • This sticker is unique to Croatia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/croatia.

metas.name: Croatia - Red Brick Architecture
metas.note:
• Buildings in Croatia sometimes feature exposed red brick walls.
  • This architecture is more common in inland areas.

--- NOTE:

  • This type of architecture can also be found in Slovenia and Serbia.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/croatia.

metas.name: Faroe Islands - Gen 4 Truck
metas.note:
• The generation 4 coverage was captured with a black pickup truck with an antenna on the front.
  • The truck is always blurred.

--- NOTE:

  • The truck in Iceland does not have a similar antenna.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Faroe Islands - Landscape
metas.note:
• The landscape of the Faroe islands is characterised by long, wide fjords with jagged green mountains that rise straight out of the water, with rocky ridge lines along the mountainsides.
  • The mountains generally look more imposing and greener than coastal mountains in Iceland, which can often be used to tell them apart.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: France - Blue Sticker
metas.note:
• Small blue rectangular markings on utility poles are unique to France.
  • They are often referred to as ‘stickers’ by the community, but are actually small plates.

--- NOTE:

  • You will find these plates on almost all wooden and metallic poles, but not as often on ladder poles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Bollards
metas.note:
• The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often.
  • It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around.
  • The band can be grey or red.
  • Some rare variations have a fully red top.

--- NOTE:

  • A bollard that is commonly found in Scotland looks similar, but has a blunt top instead of a pointed one.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Chevrons
metas.note:
• France uses chevrons with white arrows on a blue background.
  • They can have a wide amount of arrows, ranging from one to five.

--- NOTE:

  • The only other European country with this colour scheme is Spain, where you will only find chevrons with two or four arrows.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - French Pole Tops
metas.note:
• Diamond shaped pole tops with three wires are commonly called “French poletops” within the community.
  • They are most frequently found on top of ladder poles.

--- NOTE:

  • Within Europe, “French poletops” in conjunction with ladder poles are also common in Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Ladder Poles
metas.note:
• Concrete poles with step-like indents are common in France.
  • They are referred to as ladder or waffle poles by the community.

--- NOTE:

  • They are also common in Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - License Plates
metas.note:
• Modern French plates are long and white, with blue strips on both sides of the plate.
  • The left strip will be more visible than the right strip.

--- NOTE:

  • Some older French plates lack the right blue strip, with the rear plate being yellow.
  • These are very rare in newer coverage.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Long Dashed Outlines
metas.note: • Typical French roads have long spaced out dashes on the outside.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Long Middle Roadlines
metas.note:
• Middle lines with dashes that are longer than usual can be a good clue for France.

--- NOTE:

  • Unusually long dashes are also common in the UK.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Offset Block Roadlines
metas.note:
• These middle road lines, where each dash consists of two offset blocks, are unique to France.
  • They are not extremely common, but when you see them, you can safely guess France.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Rectangular Signposts
metas.note:
• Many traffic signs in France have flat rectangular signposts.
  • Signposts, along with signbacks, can be dyed with unorthodox colours, more so than in other countries.

--- NOTE:

  • The only other European countries with flat signposts are Portugal, Spain, and Andorra.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Rue
metas.note: • The French word for street is “rue”.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - Short Signposts
metas.note: • Traffic signs with particularly short signposts are very common in France.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: France - White Border Road Signs
metas.note:
• French road signs have a red border with a thin white outline.
  • You will often find white rectangular signs with black text below traffic signs.

--- NOTE:

  • Road signs in Spain have a thick red border that goes all the way to the edge.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/france.

metas.name: Gibraltar - White Tip Antenna
metas.note:
• All coverage in Gibraltar is Generation 3.
  • The car will always have a unique long antenna with a silver tip, often referred to simply as the “Gibraltar antenna” by the community.

--- NOTE:

  • This antenna can also be found in parts of Spain, but nowhere else in Europe.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Gibraltar - Yellow License Plates
metas.note:
• Like the UK, Gibraltar uses yellow back plates on vehicles.
  • However, note that unlike the UK, Gibraltar drives on the right.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Iceland - Bollards
metas.note:
• Iceland has unique yellow bollards with a white reflector.
  • These bollards are extremely common and can be found throughout the country on almost every section of rural road.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/iceland.

metas.name: Iceland - Gen 3 White Car Antenna
metas.note: • The Generation 3 Google car in Iceland is a white car with a long antenna.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/iceland.

metas.name: Iceland - Gen 4 Blurred Truck
metas.note: • The Generation 4 coverage was captured with red and white pickup trucks, which have been well blurred.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/iceland.

metas.name: Iceland - Landscape
metas.note:
• Iceland is a very geologically active country, where plate tectonics and volcanic processes have shaped the landscape.
  • As a result, many regions are rugged, mountainous and a sight to behold.
  • In addition, strange and bewildering landscapes can be found all over, such as geothermal lakes, lava fields, rift valleys, and towering rock formations.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/iceland.

metas.name: Iceland - Pedestrian Sign
metas.note:
• Icelandic pedestrian signs feature four stripes and often have a slight yellow tint.

--- NOTE:

  • Iceland is the only European country that uses pedestrian signs with a yellow background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/iceland.

metas.name: Ireland - Black Roofs
metas.note:
• You will usually find cream white buildings with black roofs in Ireland.
  • Sometimes, the buildings feature grey corner stones.
  • In cities, you will typically find row buildings.

--- NOTE:

  • British style brick buildings can still be found in Ireland.--
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Bollards
metas.note:
• These green and white bollards can be a good clue for Ireland.
  • They are not entirely unique to the country, but they are especially helpful in 50-50s with the UK.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Irish chevrons are yellow on black.
  • Both single and multiple arrows are common.

--- NOTE:

  • UK chevrons are white on black.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Diamond Warning Signs
metas.note:
• Ireland is the only European country that uses yellow diamond-shaped warning signs.

--- NOTE:

  • This only applies to warning signs.
  • Regulatory signs (circles and upside down triangles) have the normal red border and white background, like most other European countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - EU Plates
metas.note:
• Ireland has long, white licence plates with the standard European blue strip on the left.

--- NOTE:

  • The white backplate is especially useful to distinguish it from the UK, which uses yellow backplates (but white fronts).
  • In addition, most UK vehicles lack the blue strip on the left.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Pole Warning Signs
metas.note:
• The yellow warning stickers on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between Ireland and the UK.
  • The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.

--- NOTE:

  • The Irish stickers usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped.
  • They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Rounded Metal Gates
metas.note:
• Rural metal gates with rounded corners are very common in Ireland.

--- NOTE:

  • This is mainly useful to distinguish it from the UK, where similar gates typically have square corners.
  • However, gates in Northern Ireland also typically have rounded corners.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Strip Of Grass
metas.note:
• You will often see a strip of grass in the middle of tiny rural roads.
  • Such roads are called “boreens”.
  • While not unique, these boreens can often be a strong clue in a tough 50-50 between Ireland and the UK.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Yellow Dashed Outlines
metas.note:
• It is very common to see yellow outside dashes on Irish roads.

--- NOTE:

  • This is essentially never found in the UK.
  • These dashes can also be seen in New Zealand.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Ireland - Yield
metas.note:
• Irish yield signs feature the word “YIELD”.

--- NOTE:

  • UK yield signs have the phrase “GIVE WAY”.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/ireland.

metas.name: Isle of Man - Gen 2
metas.note:
• Coverage on the Isle of Man is limited to Generation 2.
  • This camera can be recognized by the lower camera quality and circular blur above and below.
  • Colours will also seem slightly off.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Isle of Man - Landscape
metas.note: • The general landscape on the Isle of Man consists of hilly farmland, and narrow roads passing through them.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Isle of Man - Red Strip Yellow Plates
metas.note: • Similar to the United Kingdom, the Isle of Man uses white front licence plates with yellow rears, but with a red strip on the left.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Italy - Architecture
metas.note:
• Italian architecture mainly consists of pastel coloured stone houses, generally with terracotta roofs.
  • Houses will very commonly have wooden shutters, which will typically be divided in two and open sideways.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Bollards
metas.note:
• Italian bollards are triangular in shape, and white with a black top.
  • They have a red front and a white rear reflector.

--- NOTE:

  • Albania uses the same bollards.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Italian chevrons are white arrows on a black background.

--- NOTE:

  • In Southern Europe, white on black chevrons can also be found in Spain, Greece and Albania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Double Guardrails
metas.note: • It is very common to find double guardrails in Italy.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Guardrail Endings
metas.note:
• Italian guardrails commonly end in this distinct shape.
  • The guardrail gets flatter, wider, and it bends away from the road.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - License Plates
metas.note:
• Contrary to most European licence plates, Italian plates have blue strips on either side of the plate.
  • Furthermore, the front plate is distinctly shorter than most European plates, which in combination with the two strips, makes it unique.

--- NOTE:

  • Albanian licence plates also have two blue strips, and French licence plates have a smaller strip on the right.
  • However, neither Albanian nor French front plates are short.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Red Reflectors
metas.note:
• Italian guardrails feature red front reflectors.

--- NOTE:

  • This is most useful to distinguish Italy from Spain, which uses yellow reflectors.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Roadlines
metas.note:
• One of the most common types of Italian road lines are white solid outer lines with no middle line.
  • This is generally less common in other Mediterranean countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Trident Pole Tops
metas.note:
• The most common pole tops in Italy are concrete trident pole tops.
  • There are several possible configurations of insulators.
  • The two shown in the image are the most common ones.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - Via & Street Signs
metas.note:
• Street signs are typically white with a thin blue border and black text.
  • The name for “Road” or “Way” in Italian is Via.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Italy - White Pole Sticker
metas.note: • Wooden poles in Italy will commonly feature a small white pole sticker.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/italy.

metas.name: Jersey - Landscape
metas.note:
• The island is shaped by a unique mix of British and Norman influences.
  • The many winding roads and hedgerows are reminiscent of English country lanes, with tree-covered roads being particularly common.
  • All images were taken by a Generation 2 camera.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Jersey - Red Granite
metas.note:
• Jersey is home to large reserves of red granite.
  • As a result, it is a popular building material used for the construction of many walls and houses throughout the island.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Luxembourg - Bollards
metas.note:
• Bollards are black and white.
  • They are wedge-shaped and have grey reflectors. Some have a distinctive indent in the lower half.

--- NOTE:

  • They look more or less identical to German bollards.
  • The most notable difference is that the reflectors on German bollards have two bolts, while in Luxembourg they have three.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/luxembourg.

metas.name: Luxembourg - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Chevrons are black with yellow arrows.
  • You may also rarely come across blue and yellow chevrons.

--- NOTE:

  • None of Luxembourg’s neighbours use these chevrons.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/luxembourg.

metas.name: Luxembourg - White Signposts
metas.note:
• Almost all Luxembourgish road signs will be supported by a white signpost.

--- NOTE:

  • While not nearly as common, white signposts are also found in France.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/luxembourg.

metas.name: Luxembourg - Yellow Plates
metas.note:
• Luxembourg uses long yellow plates with a blue strip on the left.
  • Since Luxembourg is a small country, foreign cars with white plates are somewhat common.

--- NOTE:

  • There are only a few other European countries that use yellow plates for private vehicles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/luxembourg.

metas.name: Madeira - Concrete Blocks
metas.note: • Concrete block barriers, usually painted white, are often found along roads.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Madeira - Eucalyptus Forests
metas.note:
• Similar to continental Portugal, Madeira has a lot of eucalyptus forests, which can sometimes look deceptively like the mainland.

--- NOTE:

  • The Azores do not commonly have eucalypti.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Madeira - Mountainous Landscape
metas.note:
• Madeira is a very mountainous and semi-tropical island.

--- NOTE:

  • The Azores are less mountainous and more temperate.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Madeira - Portuguese Infrastructure
metas.note: • Since Madeira is an autonomous region of Portugal, you will often come across various types of Portuguese infrastructure, such as poles and chevrons.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Madeira - Stone Bollards
metas.note:
• Madeira commonly uses small and unique stone bollards with a red reflector.
  • They are either cuboidal or cylindrical in shape.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Malta - Architecture
metas.note:
• The vast majority of buildings in Malta consist of low storey buildings, with white to beige coloured walls.
  • Buildings made of limestone are also fairly common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malta.

metas.name: Malta - Landscape
metas.note:
• The general landscape of Malta consists of slightly hilly dry agricultural fields.
  • Many roads are also only 1 or 2 lanes wide, due to the island’s size.
  • Having a mediterranean climate, cacti and various dry shrubs can be seen.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malta.

metas.name: Malta - Left Driving Side
metas.note: • Malta drives on the left.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malta.

metas.name: Malta - Rock Walls
metas.note:
• Limestone rock walls are extremely common in Malta.
  • This alone is usually enough to determine that you are in Malta.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malta.

metas.name: Malta - Triq
metas.note: • The Maltese word for street is “triq”, which can be seen on almost every street sign.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/malta.

metas.name: Monaco - Palm Trees
metas.note: • Planted palm trees are common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/monaco.

metas.name: Monaco - Vibe
metas.note:
• Monaco is a rich and densely populated city state, with a Mediterranean feel to it.
  • The architecture is similar to cities in southern France and northern Italy, but more luxurious.
  • You will see a lot of apartment buildings, neoclassical details, and pastel colours.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/monaco.

metas.name: Netherlands - Bicycle Paths
metas.note:
• Many Dutch roads are flanked by bicycle paths.
  • Different designs exist, but a very common one is a reddish-pink lane.
  • Cycling is one of the most common modes of transportation in the Netherlands.
  • You will see cyclists and bicycles everywhere.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Bollards
metas.note:
• The Netherlands has a simple, white bollard with a red reflector.

--- NOTE:

  • On rare occasions, you can find round French-style bollards with a red band and a pointed top.
  • A difference with French bollards is that the red wrap usually does not go all the way around the bollard.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Brick Roads
metas.note:
• Brick roads are common in the Netherlands, both in rural and urban areas.
  • The brick pattern shown in the image is especially common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Bulky Yellow Signposts
metas.note: • Road signs on traffic islands often have these bulky yellow signposts.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Flat Landscape
metas.note:
• The Netherlands is extraordinarily flat.
  • In most of the country, you will get no more than a few metres of elevation.
  • Large swathes of the country are reclaimed land that is at or even below sea level.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Gen 4 Black Back
metas.note: • Some Generation 4 coverage has a car blur glitch where the black back of the Google car is visible.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Large Power Lines
metas.note:
• The Netherlands usually does not have any utility poles.
  • You might see larger power lines like the ones shown in the image, but essentially never any street-level smaller utility poles.

--- NOTE:

  • Belgium does use utility poles somewhat commonly.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Rumble Strips
metas.note:
• Many rural roads feature a sort of brick rumble strip on the sides.
  • This is fairly unique to the Netherlands and a good way to identify the country in very rural rounds.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Netherlands - Yellow Plates
metas.note:
• The Netherlands has long, yellow licence plates with the standard European blue strip on the left.
  • Dutch taxis have blue plates.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/netherlands.

metas.name: Portugal - Architecture
metas.note: • White painted stone houses with orange tiled roofs are extremely common in Portugal.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Bollards
metas.note:
• Portuguese bollards are either wedge-shaped with a noticeably thin white top, or flat with a wide reflector.
  • While most reflectors will be white, you may also find orange reflectors.
  • These are noticeably darker than the yellow reflectors in Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Portuguese chevrons are black with yellow arrows.

--- NOTE:

  • Portugal is the only Mediterranean country with this chevron colour scheme.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Cobblestone Roads
metas.note:
• Cobblestone roads are very common in Portugal.
  • These will typically be made of square cobblestones arranged diagonally compared to the road direction.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Cobblestone Sidewalks
metas.note: • Similarly, cobblestone sidewalks made of distinctly bright stones are very common.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Eucalyptus Trees
metas.note:
• Eucalyptus trees are very common in Portugal.
  • The only other part of Europe where you’ll commonly see eucalyptus is northern Spain.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Hunting Signs
metas.note:
• Hunting signs with a red and white colour scheme are a common sight in rural areas.
  • They are either diamond shaped or rectangular.

--- NOTE:

  • In contrast, Spanish hunting signs are white and black.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Large Font Stop
metas.note:
• Stop signs in Portugal feature a fairly large font.

--- NOTE:

  • This is mostly useful to distinguish it from Spain, where stop signs have a distinctly small and compact font.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - License Plates
metas.note:
• Portuguese plates are long and white, with a blue strip on the left.
  • Most plates have a yellow strip on the right, which is unique to Portugal.
  • The yellow strip was discontinued in 2020, so in Generation 4 coverage you may sometimes see plates with just the blue strip.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Red Reflector
metas.note:
• Portugal uses A-type guardrails with red reflectors.

--- NOTE:

  • This is mostly useful to tell apart Portugal and Spain, which uses yellow reflectors.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Road Signs
metas.note:
• Portuguese road signs are typically encased by a white border.

--- NOTE:

  • Most Spanish signs don’t have a white border.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Rua
metas.note:
• The Portuguese word for road is ‘Rua’.

--- NOTE:

  • In Galician, the word for road is ‘Rúa’, with an accent on the ‘u’.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: Portugal - Tall Ladder Poles
metas.note:
• Concrete ladder poles, with very tall ladder steps, are common in Portugal.
  • Each step often has a small see-through hole.

--- NOTE:

  • In Spain and France you will commonly see ladder poles with short steps.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/portugal.

metas.name: San Marino - Chevrons
metas.note: • San Marino is the only country in the world to use yellow chevrons with burgundy red arrows.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/san-marino.

metas.name: San Marino - Monte Titano
metas.note:
• The 739m-tall Monte Titano dominates the surrounding landscape and is visible from almost every point in the Republic.

--- NOTE:

  • Look for the three towers to safely identify it.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/san-marino.

metas.name: Slovenia - A-Type Guardrails
metas.note:
• Slovenia uses a regular A-type guardrail, like most European countries.
  • This guardrail type has rounded edges.

--- NOTE:

  • This is mostly useful for 50-50s with Croatia, which uses B-type guardrails.
  • This type has square edges.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: Slovenia - Architecture
metas.note:
• Slovenian architecture takes much inspiration from alpine architecture, with light coloured walls, dark wooden details and semi-steep roofs.
  • The most common roof shape is half-hipped roofs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: Slovenia - Bollards
metas.note:
• Slovenian bollards are white with a black top.
  • The front reflector will typically be bright red, while the back reflector will be white.

--- NOTE:

  • Austrian bollards have the same design, but with a dark red front reflector and a black or grey back reflector.
  • Montenegrin bollards also have a very similar design, also with a red and a white reflector.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: Slovenia - Hilly Landscape
metas.note: • The Slovenian landscape is generally very hilly and forested, with occasional agriculture.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: Slovenia - House Numbers
metas.note:
• Slovenian house numbers are typically red with white text.

--- NOTE:

  • Czech house numbers are also commonly red.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: Slovenia - Kilometre Markers
metas.note:
• Slovenian kilometre markers have a very distinct design.
  • At the top left the road number is shown in a yellow rectangle, and a second number is to the right of it.
  • A horizontal black line divides the top and bottom, and the distance is shown below.

--- NOTE:

  • Austrian kilometre markers are blue with a white number.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: Slovenia - Long Dashed Outlines
metas.note:
• Slovenian roads commonly feature long outer dashes.

--- NOTE:

  • Neighbouring countries do not frequently use dashed outside lines.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/slovenia.

metas.name: Spain - Bollards
metas.note:
• The standard Spanish bollards have a yellow-orange reflector on the front and two white dots on the back (though the back can also be blank).
  • They are typically hollow.

--- NOTE:

  • Very close to Andorra, you can find a slightly different bollard, which is also used in Andorra itself.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Calle
metas.note: • The Spanish word for street is calle.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Chevrons
metas.note:
Spain has two chevrons:

  • Black with white arrows.
  • Blue with white arrows.

--- NOTE:

  • In Southern Europe, black with white chevrons can be found in Italy, Greece and Albania.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - French Pole Tops
metas.note:
• “French style” poletops are common in Spain.
  • They are shaped like an upside down triangle, with a horizontal top bar that is curved slightly upwards.
  • They are usually found on top of tall ladder poles or medium sized steel poles.

--- NOTE:

  • As the name suggests, French poletops are also very common in France.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Hunting Signs
metas.note:
• In rural areas you will often find hunting signs.
  • There are two versions, both of which are unique to Spain.
  • One is a simple white sign with a text starting with “coto” and ending in “caza”.
  • The other one has a diagonally divided black and white background.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Ladder Poles
metas.note:
• In Spain, you can find a variety of electricity poles and pole tops.
  • In small towns and sparsely populated rural areas concrete ladder poles and wooden poles are the most common.
  • “Ladder” poles have indents that resemble a ladder, hence the name.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - No Border Signs
metas.note:
• Red borders on road signs extend all the way to the edge of the sign.
  • There is no small white border separating the red part from the edge.

--- NOTE:

  • France, Italy and Portugal have a small white border on the edge of such road signs.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Pedestrian Sign
metas.note:
• Spanish pedestrian crossing signs have 8 stripes.
  • This is the highest number of stripes in Europe, and almost unique to Spain.

--- NOTE:

  • The only other European country with 8 stripes is Andorra.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Pylon Supports
metas.note: • High voltage electricity lines supported by pylons are very common in Spain, especially compared to other Mediterranean countries.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Road Markers
metas.note:
• Spain has distinct road markers with a variety of colourful borders.
  • The code on top is the number of the road.

--- NOTE:

  • Andorra has similar markers and the letter codes preceding the road number on these markers are often an important region-specific clue.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Rural Dashed Outlines
metas.note:
• Rural roads sometimes have dashed outer lines.
  • This can help tell Spain apart from Portugal and Italy, where such road lines are (almost) non-existent.

--- NOTE:

The reverse is not true:

  • Like Italy and Portugal, many Spanish roads do have solid outer lines.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Small Font Stop
metas.note:
• Spanish stop signs have a distinct small font.

--- NOTE:

  • These are mostly useful to distinguish Portugal from Spain.
  • Portuguese stop signs have a noticeably larger font.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Spain - Yellow Reflectors
metas.note:
• Spain has yellow reflectors on rounded A-type guardrails.

--- NOTE:

  • Belgium, Andorra and Gibraltar also have yellow reflectors.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/spain.

metas.name: Switzerland - Bollards
metas.note:
• Swiss bollards are black-and-white with white or grey reflectors.
  • They can be either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Switzerland - Lowcam
metas.note:
• By far the most important way to recognize Switzerland, is that all car coverage is low-cam.
  • This means that the camera on the Google car is intentionally set up lower than in most other countries.

--- THIS CAN BE RECOGNIZED IN TWO WAYS:

  • The car blur is significantly bigger.
  • Roads look wider and objects around you are seen from a lower angle.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: Switzerland - Pedestrian Sign
metas.note:
• Swiss pedestrian signs have seven stripes, making it almost unique for Europe.
  • Furthermore, rather than the typical European square shape, the signs appear as tall blue rectangles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/switzerland.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Bollards
metas.note:
• The most common bollard in the UK looks like this.
  • It has a rounded shape, with a red reflector on the front and a white one on the back.
  • The base and top are black, with a white stripe in the middle.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Cat's Eye
metas.note: • These middle lines, that consist of long dashes with cat’s eyes (reflectors) in the gaps between the dashes, are a good clue for the UK.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Chevrons
metas.note:
• Chevrons are black with white arrows.

--- NOTE:

  • Irish chevrons are black with yellow arrows.
  • French chevrons are blue with white arrows.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Give Way
metas.note:
• UK yield signs feature the phrase “GIVE WAY”.

--- NOTE:

  • Irish yields signs just have the word “YIELD”.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - License Plates
metas.note:
• UK front plates are white, while back plates are yellow.
  • Some plates have a blue strip on the left, but most do not.
  • Additionally, you might see a plate with a green ‘Zero Emissions’ strip.

--- NOTE:

  • Ireland uses white front and back plates, always with a blue strip on the left.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Pole Warning Signs
metas.note:
• The yellow warning stickers on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between the UK and Ireland.
  • The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.

--- NOTE:

  • The Irish stickers usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped.
  • They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Roadlines
metas.note:
• Double yellow road lines are often found on the sides of marked roads, especially in urban areas.
  • These lines indicate a no stopping zone.

--- NOTE:

  • These lines can also be found in Ireland.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Square Metal Gates
metas.note:
• Rural metal gates with square corners are very common in the UK.

--- NOTE:

  • This is mainly useful to distinguish it from Ireland, where similar gates typically have rounded corners.
  • Gates in Northern Ireland also typically have rounded corners.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Warning Signs
metas.note:
• Like most European countries, the UK uses triangular warning signs with a red border and a white background.

--- NOTE:

  • This is mostly useful to distinguish between the UK and Ireland, as Ireland uses diamond-shaped yellow warning signs (being the only European country to do so).
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.

metas.name: United Kingdom - Wooden Poles
metas.note:
• The UK uses wooden poles.
  • Pole steps bolted on the side of the pole are very common.
  • These pole steps are shaped like a series of thin horizontal metal rods.

--- NOTE:

  • Ireland also commonly uses wooden poles with pole steps.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: www.plonkit.net/united-kingdom.
